parsing_res_list.block_content: A message from the Moroccan front states that the artillery preparation continues, but the present operations are intended to influence the tribes now beyond French jurisdiction by the occupation of strategic positions which will assure the tribes of protection and at the same time serve as bases for mobile forces.
The grand offensive will come later and will take the rainy season into consideration. Slight rain has already fallen.

Abd el Krimi has apparently launched a counterstroke to the landing at Allucemus, according to a Madrid communiqué which says that the enemy in the western sector are still obstinately endeavouring to break through the Spanish front in the Penihozimur sector, south of Futuan. General Sons's column offered strong resistance. The conduct of the native troops was especially gallant. The enemy were provided with guns, machine guns and hand grenades.

General Primo de Riveri remains and Tetuan for the present. The communiqué states that reports from Alluenus are very satisfactory. General Sara's troops are consolidating a provisioning base and constructing defence work. The enemy's resistance is slight. The troops under General Fernandes Perez have not yet landed.

"The 'Matin's' Tannat correspondent emphasises the intensity of the artillery preparation in the general French attack on the Wezzan sector and says, never before, have so many aeroplanes been seen in the Moroccan sky, while battalion after battalion marches along the dusty roads towards this front, who would are already being sent down."

Speaking at an important meeting of the Council General of the Rhone M. Edmond Herodot said he gave his support to the Government's policy in Morocco. The Council voted unanimously a motion saying that all efforts must be made for the success of the French expedition in Morocco.

Salt Lake City, Sept. 10. Mr. Smoot, Chairman of the American Debt Funding Commission, in an address here, declared that France cannot hope for a more favourable settlement of her debt to America than was awarded to Britain. She cannot presume that the United States will accept any plan formulated by the recent conference between Mr. Churchill, British Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Caillaux, French Finance Minister.

The Government's financial advisers recommended the restoration of the gold standard and the preparation of a new monetary law in accordance with the recently drawn up proposals.
It is proposed that the par value of the Finnish mark shall be 39/70 for the gold dollar.

It is semi-officially denied that there is an epidemic of plague at Marseilles, and it is pointed out that a few isolated cases occurred in the summer but at present the situation is quite satisfactory.

London, September 10.—The report has been denied that Japanese salvores are preparing to attempt to recover the gold from the Peninsular and Oriental liner Egypt, which sank in May, 1922, off Ushant. On the contrary a French firm is under-taking the work, with German sub-conditioning carrying out the actual diving operations, using a special diving lease for great depth. It is noteworthy that the Egypt carried £1,089,000, of which £830,000 was gold.—Reuter
The police have unearthed a complete list of members of the Fiery Cross mentioned earlier and have instructed the authorities all over the country to arrest all of the members.
The arrested include the well-known Nationalists ex-Lieutenant Hildebrandt, Dr, Huebner, and ex-Captain Klipproth.
The last-named was apprehended on the point of crossing the frontier into Holland in a motor car.
It appears the order was found-ed two years ago and played a great part in the revolt of the so-called Black Reichswehr which started in 1923 in the fortresses of Cuestrin and Spandau.

Thirty "Knights of the Fiery Cross" were arrested by the police who claim that they have discovered a dangerous extremist organisation of a thousand members. The founders of the new order are three Americans who are among the arrested men. They came to Germany to create an organisation on the lines of the Ku Klux Klan in order to liberate Germany from persons not "100 per cent. true Germans."
A hundred strikers of various vessels have been sentenced to a fortnight's or three weeks' imprisonment for disobedience of lawful commands.

Wellington, Sept. 10.
Twenty-eight seamen of the liner "Port Dunedin" have been sentenced to a month's imprisonment.
A number of strikers of the steamer "Benecia" have been ordered to forfeit 5s. for every day's absence from their duties.
The British shipowners have cabled that they are prepared to continue to pay allotment money to the strikers' families if the men will return to full duty under the present articles.
Further convictions involving imprisonment have been obtained against disobedient seamen, including negroes, at Sydney.

Telegrams to the American legation from Harbin state that the terms with regard to Mr. Howard's release have now been arranged with the bandits' leader who is expected to arrive at Huachuan to-day to complete the final negotiations.
Some delay, however, is regarded as inevitable in view of the difficulties attending communication between the bandit leader and his camp.

League control in Austria has considerably diminished by the end of the year. League's High Commissioner, Mr. Zimmerman, will leave Vienna in accordance with the Financial Committee's report recommending the gradual abolition of League control, though on Mr. Austen Chamberlain's proposal Australia will undertake not to oppose the reintroduction of control in the event of her failure to fulfil her obligations under the League.

Two aviators' coats and two life-preserving jackets marked United States Navy have been found at different places along the coast near Hilo.
They are supposed to be a clue to the fate of the crew of the missing' seaplane. The Navy search continues.

A cable dated September 2, stated: — Five men in a disabled seaplane in a rough sea drenched by a tropical storm is the picture evoked by reports of the warships searching in mid-Pacific for seaplane P59, No. 1, one of the two that started to fly to Hawaii. She wirelessed that she would probably be forced to descend at 1.45 p.m. yesterday, 150 knots from the island of Maui, owing to adverse winds and lack of fuel. "We shall crack up if we come down in this weather," was almost the last message received from the plane.
A scheme for defrauding the Revenue Department was disclosed at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday when Tang Hon, a Chinese revenue officer, was charged with intimidation.

The story as outlined by Mr. T. S. Whyte-Smith for the prosecution was that the complainant, Wong Yuet, owner of the Woo Sung Distillery of Cheung Sha Wan, had been threatened by the accused with bodily harm if he refused to submit to a scheme for defrauding the Government of duty. Green labels were affixed to bottles of wine leaving the distillery, and the Crown suggested that the scheme was to send the bottles to dealers and then remove the labels, which would be taken back to the distillery to be used again.

Leave of appeal was granted in the Supreme Court yesterday in respect of a case in which Mr. Justice Wood had held against a broker who sued another broker on the grounds that he had broken a contract in not taking up 100 Shanghai Dock shares.

One particular point stressed by Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., who appeared for the petitioner for the appeal, was that Mr. Justice Wood had held for the contract to be binding that an exchange rate for the transaction should be fixed a week before settlement day. The meaning of this term in the contract, said Sir Henry, was that the exchange was to be ascertained one week before settlement day, that was to say the current rate for that day to be ascertained for the purpose of converting itself into Hongkong dollars.
There were other points but he had not been able to get a copy of the judge's notes, said counsel (who was instructed by Mr. G. R. Haywood).

Mr. and Mrs. David Harvey, of Aima Villas, Kowloon, entertained a large number of friends at a party at the Station Hotel yesterday evening, in celebration of their silver wedding. They were the recipients of congratulations upon this happy event which took place at the Union Church, Kowloon, both having resided in the Colony for nearly 80 years.

Mr. and Mrs. C. H. Lammert also celebrated their silver wedding yesterday. Mr. Lammert has resided in Hongkong since the attack on Shameen where he was at the time carrying on business as an exchange broker. The wedded took place at Shanghai. From a correspondent who signs himself "J.C." we have received a letter dealing with local problems of the first importance. Owing to the pressure on our space to-day we are unable to publish the letter in full. Referring to the growing atmosphere of "tiredness and drift," J.C. writes:

"There is no excuse for any policy of drift, or for any easing down of our standards as regards the governance of the Colony. In one's wanderings round the city in the course of the day, one seems to notice everywhere a slovenliness and a slackness in the way that public work is being carried on. For example, the streets, before the strike, were always clean and well swept. Now, particularly at tram stops, they look as if they were never swept, or as if the cleaning up and washing away of rubbish depended on the wind and rain. Let one cast one's eyes up the side streets when going along the Praya East on a tram, and notice what a fearful state some of them are in. Not to spin out, what I have said about street cleaning, applies to most of the jobs that are in progress."

"Now let us leave the present and take a long view of the future of Hongkong. Surely by now the Government must have realised the public are not children and that it is quite safe to take them into their confidence as regards the broad outlines of their policy. We all applauded when the rounding up policy was inaugurated, and we can all see what a beneficial effect it has had, particularly in the criminal courts. What we would all like to know—and undoubtedly we are entitled to know—is what the policy is going to be in the future. Are we going to drift back to that miserable policy of admitting the lame, the halt and the blind, the criminals and Bolsheviks, who all make of Hongkong a happy hunting ground? Or are we going to continue the policy of frequent cleanups, followed by the deportation of undesirables? What is the real objection to a poll-tax?"

J.C. points out that the French and Americans are both able to collect a poll tax in neighbouring colonies and suggests that the revenue, amounting to millions even with the poll tax as low as $2 per head, would go a long way to fill “the nasty gap” the depression will make in the Colony's revenue.

"Is one a pessimist if one assumes that British business houses, both old and new, are going to be very badly hit in some cases, perhaps, even to drop out?" J.C. asks next. "Granted that, it means a big reduction of staffs, from top to bottom. One knows, also, that a very large proportion of British coast shipping is laid up, and that Norwegian, Japanese and others have got such a footing that it will be a long time before British shipping is running again at any profit. That means, in conjunction with the starvation wages paid in Norwegian and Japanese ships, that there will be any number of Britishers out of jobs on the China Coast."

Is it not time that some notice was taken of the increasing numbers of Russians who are flocking into the Colony? There was a time when Russians were forbidden to land here on the ground that Hongkong did not wish to have to face the problem that Shanghai was up against. It is quite time that our own problem of what is going to happen to our own people, who will be axed, during the coming winter, were thoroughly gone into. After pointing to the fact that Russians are doing work which could be done by Britons, J.C. remarks: It is quite time that the Government began to get busy on this problem of unemployment. They have the example of Singapore before them, and there is at present nothing to show that Hongkong may not have to endure just as long and severe a storm as Singapore faced, with practically the same problems.
"Turning to another side of the problem, are the public not entitled to know what the Government are doing to trim ship and shorten sail, to meet the storm? After the recent inquests, with the summings up and the Juries riders, we all know that things in the P.W.D. are pretty rotten. Is the Government going to ignore the suggestion for an expert's inquiry into the working of the P.W.D.? With the lean times ahead, such inquiry should be extended into the whole question of whether the Colony is getting anything. After encountering adverse weather at different stages of the voyage from the American Pacific coast, the R.M.S. "Empress of Russia" arrived here at 7.30 this morning with mails, passengers and cargo.
In the report to the Harbour Office it is stated: Encountered typhoon weather off Nagasaki.

According to advice from Shanghai she was kept back for 15 hours by that storm and another typhoon off Woosung the last week-end added to the delay. The scheduled date of arrival here was September 7.

In the Northern typhoon of last week-end grave fears were entertained for the N.Y.K. steamer "Yoshino Maru" which was in the middle of the depression. She sent out a wireless S.O.S. which was answered by the U.S.S. "Noa."
Besides hindering the “Empress of Russia” the typhoon also held up the “Empress of Canada” which left Hongkong for Shanghai, and did not arrive in time.

Just two years ago, Mr. L. M. Karukhan was met in Harbin, on his arrival from Moscow, by an enormous crowd of people. He was yesterday greeted by the Soviet citizens's of Harbin in such a manner as Kings and Emperors are accustomed to. A special train of eight cars, including the now celebrated No 56, was sent specially to Chingchun to bring him to Harbin and many representatives of the Russian Consulate and the C. B. R. went to meet him. Thousands of people crowded the roads to the Harbin railway station and literally hundreds of motor cars fought their way through the crowd. As the train steamed into the station, the symphony orchestra played the strains of the "International" and all eyes were fixed on car 56, where, however, only a Russian soldier was to be seen. Mr. Karukhan and suite happened to be in the observation car at the end of the train. As he descended from the curring, the air was rent with motor sirens and horns and the hurrabs of the thousands of people. He entered the large arrival room where fruit and champagne were served and he was introduced to heads of the Railway Departments and to the Chinese administrative chiefs. During this reception the brass band from the Railway Club played selections. After a quarter of an hour, the police made a road for the Soviet ambassador and his family, who entered motor cars and drove to a railway house which has been put at his disposal. Last night a banquet was served at the Chinese Administration quarters, and to-day there are three special fetings to Mr. Karakhan. The first is a lunch at the Railway Workman's Club, the first that this Club has ever given, the second a five o'clock ten at the Railway Club for the hands of all the railway departments and this evening a grand banquet at the Railway Club. To-morrow morning Mr. Karakhan leaves for Moscow, travelling in the special train as far as the frontier and in his special car right through to the end of the journey. The fitting up of this car has cost the C. B. R. a sum of thirty thousand dollars and no crowned head, has ever had such a sumptuous carriage to travel in.
